original_requirement: Cautiously hawkish but divided. As of October 21, 1962, the American public is largely unaware of the secret missile crisis (the administration has not yet informed them of the Soviet missiles in Cuba):contentReference[oaicite:33]{index=33}. Generally, public sentiment supports a tough U.S. stance against any Soviet weapons in Cuba – reflecting anger at the idea of a Soviet threat so close to home and a belief in defending the Monroe Doctrine principle:contentReference[oaicite:34]{index=34}. original_requirement: Patriotic anti-communism mixed with survival instincts. The American public in 1962 broadly endorses the Cold War consensus of containing communism – they do not want the Soviet Union installing offensive weapons in the Western Hemisphere and many feel the U.S. must assert its power. At the same time, average citizens are acutely aware of the horrors of nuclear war (doing "duck and cover" drills and building fallout shelters). Thus, their “ideology” is not monolithic: it’s a mix of strong anti-Soviet, pro-national security sentiment and a hope to live in peace. They support the idea of the U.S. standing tough ("not appeasing" Moscow), but also favor any solution that can resolve the crisis without war, reflecting a practical desire to survive.
